## Pivotting data: wide vs long {#sec-pivot}

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

### Data

# CO2 data from Global Carbon Budget (2025); Jones et al. (2025) – with major processing by Our World in Data
temp <- read_csv("data/temperature_anomaly.csv")
table(temp$region)
ggplot(temp, aes(x=year, y=temp_anomaly, color=region)) + 
  geom_line()  


### Using pivot_wider

# (2) We notice a gap between south and north, this is a good usecase for teaching pivot_wider:
temp_diff <- temp |> 
  select(year, region, temp_anomaly) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from=region, values_from=temp_anomaly) |>
  rename(south=`Southern Hemisphere`, north=`Northern Hemisphere`) |>
  mutate(diff=north - south) 

temp_diff |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=diff)) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="red", alpha=.2) + 
  geom_line()

# Add a callout on the imporance of selecting out any columns with variation

### Using pivot_longer

# Just to teach the syntax, let's reverse the pivot_wider
pivot_longer(temp_diff, north:diff)
pivot_longer(temp_diff, -year, names_to="region", values_to="temperature_anomaly")


### Carbon dioxide data

# For a more serious use of pivot_longer let's have a look at the carbon data
co2  <- read_csv("data/co2_emissions.csv")
# Note: We remove 'world' from the csv so we can reinforce the groupby_summarize
co2 |> 
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(co2=sum(co2, na.rm=TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=co2)) + geom_line()

#  plot the co2, methane, no and ghg 
# This requires pivot_longer (to use color=variable)
ghg_sources <- co2 |>
  select(country, year, co2, methane, nitrous_oxide) |>
  pivot_longer(co2:nitrous_oxide, names_to="source")

ghg_sources |> 
  group_by(year, source) |>
  summarize(value=sum(value, na.rm=TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=value, color=source)) + geom_line()

# Callout on 'tidy' data, esp for ggplot
```



## Joining multiple data sets

Claude: 
- 1:many blowup needs to be singalled explicitly
- coverage loss for income classification is a good explicit lesson
- order bar plot

```{r}
# Are the rich or the poor countrires polluting?
# Let's get income class data
income <- read_csv("data/income_groups.csv")
income_2020 <- income |> filter(Year==2020) |> select(country=Entity, income=`World Bank's income classification`)

# Cutoff at 2020 and join
# Naive: inner join

co2_2020 <- co2 |> filter(year == 2020)
combined <- inner_join(co2_2020, income_2020) 
ggplot(combined, aes(y=income, x=cumulative_co2)) + geom_col()
# Note: Should summarize first!

# Callout (or challenge) on key columns and renaming/selecting (preferred) vs using by


### Explaining inner / full / left / right
combined_left <- left_join(co2_2020, income_2020) 
filter(combined_left, is.na(income))

### Explain semi and anti join as useful shorthand and debugging tools
anti_join(co2_2020, income_2020)
semi_join(co2_2020, income_2020)

# challenge to interpret this, especially venezuela,
# and figure out a way of dealing with it

### Exercise: co2 by country income type over time
income |> select(country=Entity, year=Year, income=`World Bank's income classification`) |>
  inner_join(co2) |>
  group_by(year, income) |>
  summarize(co2=sum(co2, na.rm=T)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=co2, fill=income)) + geom_area()

# Challenge: why are low-income countries emitting less co2 over time?
# what is the bump in upper-middle countries in 2010? (answer: countries (esp china) are reclassified)
# How could you fix this? (answer: use a constant measure, e.g. use the 2020 classification instead)
# what changes if you use cumulative co2 instead? (answer: it makes the rich world's share clearer)
```

## Exercise: Are co2 emissions and temperature correlated over time?

(chapter-level exercise combining joining and pivoting)

```{r}
# Part A: Join
world_temp <- temp |> filter(region == "World")
world_co2 <- co2 |> group_by(year) |> summarize(co2=sum(cumulative_co2, na.rm=TRUE))
temp_and_co2 <- inner_join(world_temp, world_co2) 
cor.test(temp_and_co2$temp_anomaly, temp_and_co2$co2)

# Part B: Pivot to plot
temp_and_co2 |> select(year, co2, temp_anomaly) |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  mutate(index=value/mean(value) * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=index, color=name)) + geom_line() 

# Challenge: is the correlation actually meaningful? How to fix this?
```
